summary.headline: A cash-rich coconut estate with a strong balance sheet, but the price is more than double fair value and the land leases end in 2028–29
summary.text: Mahaweli Coconut Plantations (MCPL.N0000) grows coconuts on 551 hectares of Mahaweli Authority land at Pimburettewa in the dry zone (Polonnaruwa), irrigated by drip and solar pumps, and sells about 3.2–3.8 million nuts a year to desiccated coconut makers, plus some copra, coir, coco peat and teak. It is a small company (35.0m shares, about Rs 1.6bn market value) owned mostly by coconut millers, with no controlling shareholder. Profit after tax has swung between Rs 36m and Rs 191m over ten years: Rs 140m in 2024/25 and Rs 121m in 2025/26 (EPS Rs 3.46) at a record coconut price of Rs 128.52 a nut. The first half of 2026/27 brought a loss of Rs 13m (EPS −Rs 0.38) as cost of sales rose 62% while revenue fell 3% in a severe drought. The balance sheet is strong: about Rs 427m of cash and deposits and no bank debt, so roughly Rs 9 a share is net cash after the Rs 3.00 dividend for 2025/26 (ex-dividend 1 October 2026). The big risk is the land: the three leases end in March 2028, November 2028 and August 2029, and one has never been signed by the Mahaweli Authority; the company expects renewal but hasn't started talks. At Rs 45.10 (CSE close on 13 November 2026, after the dividend) the share trades at 23x trailing earnings of Rs 1.96, 13x the 2025/26 earnings and 2.1x NAV of Rs 21.91, yielding 6.7%. Four methods put fair value at about Rs 21.67: a business that earns around Rs 110m in a normal year is worth roughly Rs 0.8bn at the 16% return I ask, not Rs 1.6bn. Three of four business tests pass, so it counts as a good business, but the price is far too high: buy only up to Rs 18.42, strong buy under Rs 16.25.

quality.reason: No debt, a cash pile and profit that turns into cash and dividends; returns averaged about 17% over five years but are falling, and profit swings widely with weather and coconut prices. The tests don't capture the land lease risk (expiry 2028–29).

tests.label: Return on equity of 15% or more
tests.note: 27%, 10%, 17%, 16% and 14% (Annual Report 2025/26, p. 131, ten-year summary). Falling: about 9% in the 12 months to September 2026. A marginal pass; equity includes about Rs 0.4bn of cash and deposits earning interest.

tests.label: Net debt no more than equity
tests.value: Net cash about Rs 0.41bn vs equity Rs 0.75bn
tests.note: Cash Rs 10.5m and short-term deposits Rs 416.9m against only Rs 16.7m of land lease liabilities and no bank overdraft at 30 September 2026 (Interim Q2 2026/27, p. 1). About Rs 105m of that pays the 2025/26 dividend in October 2026.

tests.label: Steady profit: no loss in five years, no one-offs
tests.value: Rs 70m–191m a year; loss in H1 2026/27
tests.note: Profit after tax Rs 191m (2021/22), 70m, 136m, 140m and 121m (2025/26), Annual Report p. 131. No full-year loss, but profit fell 64% in 2022/23, and the six months to September 2026 lost Rs 13.2m in a drought (Interim p. 2). Teak revaluation gains (Rs 7.6m, 19.7m) and a Rs 9.0m unclaimed-dividend write-back help some years.

tests.label: Profit turns into cash and dividends
tests.value: Operating cash Rs 1.07bn vs profit Rs 1.11bn over ten years
tests.note: Ten-year operating cash flow is 96% of profit (Annual Report p. 131). 2025/26: Rs 89m against profit Rs 121m because Rs 85m of tax was paid, including the previous year's (Rs 7m in 2024/25). Dividends paid every year.

valuation.note: Fair value weights the bear/base/bull averages of four methods 30/50/20 (about 6.9x base normal EPS of Rs 3.14, or 1.0x NAV). NAV of Rs 21.91 includes about Rs 9 of net cash and Rs 6.69 of teak at fair value.

dividend.label: final for 2025/26
dividend.source: Annual Report 2025/26, pp. 9, 11 and 138 (notice of meeting)
dividend.note: Approved at the AGM on 30 September 2026; ex-dividend 1 October 2026. Rs 3.00 final for 2024/25 as well (paid in 2025/26, Annual Report p. 96). One final dividend a year; no interims.

highlights.title: April–September 2026 (unaudited)
highlights.text: Revenue down 3% to Rs 189.6m, but cost of sales up 62% to Rs 207.1m, so a gross loss of Rs 17.5m (gross profit Rs 67.9m a year earlier). Administration costs up 22%. Loss Rs 13.2m (EPS −Rs 0.38) against a profit of Rs 39.1m. Q2 alone: revenue Rs 96.5m (+3%), profit Rs 4.5m (−84%). The report gives no reason for the cost jump; the annual report warned of a severe dry-zone drought from May 2026 (no rain from 18 May to 31 August) and a lower 2026/27 crop.

highlights.title: 2025/26 (audited)
highlights.text: Record revenue of Rs 456.9m (+10%) as the average coconut price rose 15% to Rs 128.52 a nut on a flat crop of 3.76m nuts. Gross margin fell to 36.3% from 48.6% on higher wages, maintenance and harvesting costs and cyclone Ditwah damage. Profit Rs 121.0m (−14%), EPS Rs 3.46. Dividend Rs 3.00 (about 87% of profit).

highlights.title: Land leases end 2028–29
highlights.text: The 551 hectares are held under three Mahaweli Authority leases ending 31 March 2028 (129 ha, never signed by the Authority), 30 November 2028 (292 ha) and 31 August 2029 (130 ha). The company rates this a high risk, says such leases are generally extended, and plans to start renewal talks in the expiry year (Annual Report pp. 46 and 110).

highlights.title: Water tax and fertiliser
highlights.text: The Mahaweli Authority plans to charge for irrigation water; the cost can't yet be estimated. Fertiliser reached only 60% of palms in 2025/26 because of supply problems and a March 2026 ban on fertiliser issues by private companies (Annual Report pp. 9–11, 17).

highlights.title: Cash and teak
highlights.text: Cash and deposits of Rs 427m at September 2026 (about Rs 12 a share; about Rs 9 after the October dividend) and 22,153 teak trees valued at Rs 234m (Rs 6.69 a share), sold gradually.

methodReadings.reading: High for a single-crop estate whose profit swings with rain and coconut prices; 9x at March 2025.
NAV of Rs 21.91 is mostly cash, teak and irrigation assets; paying 2.1x book for returns of 9–14% doesn't add up.
About 17% on average over five years, falling to 9% in the last 12 months; diluted by a large cash holding.
Rs 3.00 for each of the last two years, close to 90% of profit; likely lower for 2026/27 after the first-half loss.
Before interest income; about 3–7% of the market value.
After the October 2026 dividend; a cushion, but only a fifth of the price.

models.name: Free cash flow DCF + net cash
models.comment: Operating free cash flow (before interest income) of Rs 45m / 75m / 95m a year plus about Rs 305m net cash after the 2025/26 dividend. Bear: leases not renewed, so three more years of cash, the teak sold (Rs 234m less 30% tax) and the cash returned. Base/bull: leases renewed, growth 3% / 4% for ever. Cost of equity 17% / 16% / 15%.

models.name: P/E method
models.comment: Normal profit Rs 70m / 110m / 140m (EPS Rs 2.00 / 3.14 / 4.00) at 6 / 8 / 10 times. The justified P/E for a 90% payout, 3% growth and a 16% return is about 7x.

models.name: Dividend model
models.comment: Dividend Rs 1.50 / 2.75 / 3.25 a share; growth 0% / 3% / 4% for ever; cost of equity 17% / 16% / 15%. Rs 3.00 was paid for each of the last two years.

models.name: Residual income
models.comment: NAV Rs 21.91 plus the value of earning Rs 2.00 / 3.14 / 4.00 a share on it against a 17% / 16% / 15% cost of equity, with the excess growing 1% / 3% / 4%. Normal returns of 9–14% are below the cost of equity in bear and base, so value is below book.

modelsNote: A small cash generator that pays out most of its profit, so value comes from cash flow, dividends and earnings, with residual income as a check against book value. The lease expiry in 2028–29 is handled in the bear case (no renewal). All four methods are far below the price.

scenarios.common: 10-year government bond about 12% plus 3–5 points for a small, thinly traded single-crop company with lease and weather risk. Tax 30%. Profit averaged Rs 111m over ten years and Rs 132m over five, in years that included record coconut prices, so the base takes Rs 110m as normal. Net cash Rs 305m after the 2025/26 dividend. Shares 34,996,115.

sensitivity.title: Free cash flow DCF + net cash (3% growth), Rs per share
sensitivity.note: Even at 15% and Rs 95m a year the DCF gives Rs 32, well below Rs 45.10. The price needs about Rs 160m of free cash a year for ever at 16%, twice the base, or a cost of equity near 9%. If the leases are not renewed the value falls to about Rs 15.

buyPlan.note: About Rs 9,535 in total, against Rs 22,550 at Rs 45.10. Trading is thin (about 4m shares traded in 2025/26), so use limit orders.
buyPlan.realism: Not realistic soon: the lowest price in April 2024–September 2026 was Rs 25.10 (2024/25), and Rs 32.00 in 2025/26. It would take a sharp fall in coconut prices, a lease problem or a weak market.

higher: Clear renewal of all three land leases for another 30 years on similar rent.
Coconut prices staying near Rs 120+ a nut while the crop recovers to 4.5m+ nuts with full fertiliser.
The water tax being dropped or set low.
Coir, coco peat and cinnamon growing into a real second business.
A special dividend or other return of the surplus cash.
lower: Any sign the Mahaweli Authority won't renew the leases, or wants much higher rent.
More drought (El Niño) cutting the 2026/27 crop, as the first-half loss suggests.
Coconut prices falling back as national output recovers.
A heavy water tax or rising wages squeezing margins further.

notes.disclaimer: These are estimates from the 2025/26 annual report and the interim report to 30 September 2026 (unaudited). The price used is the CSE close on 13 November 2026. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.

Decision box.Verdict: Overpriced: about 108% above fair value of Rs 21.67.
Decision box.Downside / upside: Bear case Rs 11.73; bull case Rs 33.38 (both well below the price).
Decision box.What the price assumes: Profit of about Rs 180–220m a year for good (above any year but 2021/22), or investors accepting a return of about 10% (6.7% yield plus 3% growth), below government bonds.
Decision box.Confidence: Low to medium: profit swings with weather and coconut prices, and the land leases end in 2028–29.
Decision box.Margin of safety: Buy 15% below fair value (Rs 18.42), strong buy 25% below (Rs 16.25).

Business and moat.What it does: Grows coconuts on 551 hectares of irrigated dry-zone land at Pimburettewa, Aralaganwila (about 74,000 palms, 51 nuts a tree in 2025/26), and sells them mainly to desiccated coconut mills, many of them shareholders. Small side lines: copra, coir, coco peat and coco chips (Rs 22m revenue), teak, cinnamon, pepper and areca nut. Largest supplier of seed nuts to the Coconut Cultivation Board.
Business and moat.Moat: Weak: a price-taker in a commodity, with no say over the land, water price or fertiliser supply. Advantages are good irrigation and yields above the coconut triangle average.

Management and governance.Ownership: Widely held: the 20 largest shareholders own 53%, mostly coconut millers and their owners; public 90.83% (1,310 public shareholders, September 2026). Listed on the Diri Savi board.
Management and governance.Leadership: Managing Director/CEO J F Fernandopulle; directors hold about 7.8% between them.
Management and governance.Related parties: Sells coconuts to companies linked to directors and shareholders (e.g. Rs 23.7m to Baduwatta DC Mills in the September quarter, Interim p. 5).

Sri Lanka checks.Land: Mahaweli Authority leases ending 31 March 2028, 30 November 2028 and 31 August 2029; the 129-hectare lease was never signed by the Authority (Annual Report p. 110).
Sri Lanka checks.Policy: Planned water tax on irrigation; March 2026 ban on fertiliser issues by private companies (Annual Report pp. 9–11).

What this analysis doesn't cover: Why cost of sales rose 62% in April–September 2026 (not explained in the interim report); crop and nut prices for the half.
Any progress on renewing the land leases or on the water tax.
fullText:
Mahaweli Coconut Plantations (MCPL.N0000) grows coconuts on 551 hectares of Mahaweli Authority land at Pimburettewa in the dry zone (Polonnaruwa), irrigated by drip and solar pumps, and sells about 3.2–3.8 million nuts a year to desiccated coconut makers, plus some copra, coir, coco peat and teak. It is a small company (35.0m shares, about Rs 1.6bn market value) owned mostly by coconut millers, with no controlling shareholder. Profit after tax has swung between Rs 36m and Rs 191m over ten years: Rs 140m in 2024/25 and Rs 121m in 2025/26 (EPS Rs 3.46) at a record coconut price of Rs 128.52 a nut. The first half of 2026/27 brought a loss of Rs 13m (EPS −Rs 0.38) as cost of sales rose 62% while revenue fell 3% in a severe drought. The balance sheet is strong: about Rs 427m of cash and deposits and no bank debt, so roughly Rs 9 a share is net cash after the Rs 3.00 dividend for 2025/26 (ex-dividend 1 October 2026). The big risk is the land: the three leases end in March 2028, November 2028 and August 2029, and one has never been signed by the Mahaweli Authority; the company expects renewal but hasn't started talks. At Rs 45.10 (CSE close on 13 November 2026, after the dividend) the share trades at 23x trailing earnings of Rs 1.96, 13x the 2025/26 earnings and 2.1x NAV of Rs 21.91, yielding 6.7%. Four methods put fair value at about Rs 21.67: a business that earns around Rs 110m in a normal year is worth roughly Rs 0.8bn at the 16% return I ask, not Rs 1.6bn. Three of four business tests pass, so it counts as a good business, but the price is far too high: buy only up to Rs 18.42, strong buy under Rs 16.25.

Valuation table (Rs per share)
Method | Bear | Base | Bull | Weighted
Free cash flow DCF + net cash | 14.98 | 25.70 | 34.38 | 24.22
P/E method | 12.00 | 25.15 | 40.00 | 24.17
Dividend model | 8.82 | 21.79 | 30.73 | 19.69
Residual income | 11.13 | 19.12 | 28.40 | 18.58
Average | 11.73 | 22.94 | 33.38 | 21.67

Fair value Rs 21.67 (bear 30 / base 50 / bull 20). Buy price Rs 18.42 (15% below), strong buy Rs 16.25 (25% below).

How the business works: the estate harvests coconuts six times a year from about 74,000 palms on irrigated dry-zone land and sells them, mostly to desiccated coconut mills. Revenue depends on the crop (3.7–5.5m nuts a year over the last decade) and the nut price, which reached a record Rs 128.52 in 2025/26 as national output fell short of demand. Costs are mostly wages, fertiliser, irrigation and harvesting, so a poor crop hits profit hard, as in the first half of 2026/27.

Why the methods are so far below the price: in a normal year the company earns about Rs 110m (Rs 3.14 a share) including interest on its cash. At the 16% return I ask, that is worth about Rs 20–26 a share, plus or minus the cash. At Rs 45.10 the market pays 23x the last 12 months' earnings and 13x a record-price year.

The leases: all the land is leased from the Mahaweli Authority and the three leases end between March 2028 and August 2029. The company expects renewal; if they weren't renewed, shareholders would get roughly the cash, the teak and two or three more years of profit, about Rs 15 a share.

Dividends: Rs 3.00 for 2025/26 (ex-dividend 1 October 2026) and Rs 3.00 for 2024/25, about 87% of profit. After the first-half loss, a smaller dividend for 2026/27 is likely.

Buy plan: 200 shares up to Rs 21.67, 150 up to Rs 18.42 and 150 up to Rs 16.25, about Rs 9,535 in total (average Rs 19.07), against Rs 22,550 at Rs 45.10. Not realistic soon: the lowest price since April 2024 was Rs 25.10.

Business tests: 3 of 4 passed (returns, debt, cash; profit is not steady), so it's a good business at a price far too high: watch list (category 2).

Uncertain: the interim report doesn't explain the 62% rise in cost of sales. Dividend payable of about Rs 105m appears to sit in trade payables at 30 September 2026, inflating first-half operating cash flow. Return on equity for 2025/26 is 13.92% in the key highlights and 14% in the ten-year summary. Owner's note on the request ('.N00') looked like part of the code and was ignored.
